newsitem.title: KAZAKHSTAN: Kazakhstan takes first steps towards stock market.
newsitem.headline: Kazakhstan takes first steps towards stock market.

text.p: Resource-rich Kazakhstan, which aims to set up a viable securities market by the end of the year, has started setting up the infrastructure to attract foreign investors.

"I think Kazakhstan's securities market will start developing rapidly in the second half of this year," Grigory Marchenko, chairman of the National Securities Market Commission, told a news conference late on Tuesday.
Local experts say the Central Asian state's present stock market is lifeless because infrastructure is inadequate and there are no liquid shares.
But Marchenko said the National (central) Bank and the Kazakh Stock Exchange had already been selected to set up a central depository of securities compatible with international standards.
He also said some 90 local broker and dealer companies had been given three months to boost their capital to at least $130,000 from present-day $20,000.
"The new demand has been correctly understood by the participants of the securities market," said Marchenko.
The final goal is to boost capital of brokers and dealers to $1 million "to attract serious foreign investors".
"Those with a capital of $130,000 will be eventually limited to working only with local investors," he said.
Attracting foreign investors to Kazakhstan's securities market is a priority for Marchenko.
"In the first stage... foreign investors will be the main source of investment on our market of corporate securities," Marchenko said.
He added: "It would take up two years before local private persons regain confidence in the state, take their savings from under mattresses and start investing in Kazakh corporate paper".
The authorities have so far selected over 50 large local companies whose shares will be offered to foreign investors.

Many of these companies -- seen by the authorities as future Kazakh "blue chips" -- are involved in the extraction and processing of Kazakhstan's rich natural resources, as well as its energy and communications sector.

Marchenko said the government, alongside the World Bank's private-sector affiliate, the International Finance Corporation, and the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development, was planning to hold in June this year an international seminar at which heads of these companies would meet potential investors.
"But many local directors simply do not know what demands will be applied by foreign investors to their companies," he said.
He said the government had demanded that local companies bring accounts into line with international standards and order international audits of their activities last year.

The approval of bills on the securities market, investment funds and registration of deals with securities already under discussion in parliament is likely to speed up the creation of a real stock market in Kazakhstan, Marchenko said.
